title: What is known about 1RB1LB_1LC0RD_0LE1LA_0RF1RA_1LE0LA_---0RB
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LB_1LC0RD_0LE1LA_0RF1RA_1LE0LA_---0RB.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The sweep rule is now decoded: writing x = 111 and y = 110, one right sweep and one left sweep over a clean word string replace each word by the XOR of it and its right neighbour (x = 0, y = 1), the linear cellular automaton known as rule 102, checked exhaustively for every string up to 16 words. Every word string is therefore possible in the bulk, and halting depends only on the defects (alignment walls) that the small structure at the right end emits. No closed tape language has been found.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: Where a halt can come from
claims.text: If the machine halts on its third step from a configuration, that configuration is one of: B with 1 under the head, 0 right, 0 two right. So a run can reach a halt only through one of these patterns, and a proof that the machine never halts only has to rule them out. The proof splits on the state and the five cells around the head.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 43,577 cells have been visited and 35,099 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.505). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.067).

claims.title: Shift rules over 3-cell words
claims.text: Ten rules, each for every n and every surrounding tape: for example D turns (101)<sup>n</sup> into (110)<sup>n</sup> going right, B turns (110)<sup>n</sup> into (011)<sup>n</sup>, A runs left over (110)<sup>n</sup> turning it into (111)<sup>n</sup>.

claims.title: The string is rewritten every sweep
claims.text: At successive visits of the head to the left end (steps 2,918,884 … 2,994,219) the left string is different each time, not shifted copies of one another, and the visited width grows by one or two cells per visit (2,366 → 2,395 in 29 visits). Read as words of 3 cells it is a string over 110 and 111.

claims.title: Regular-language deciders tried (F11)
claims.text: None of these closes: each reaches a halting configuration in its abstraction, which says nothing about whether the machine halts. n-gram CPS (tools/c/ngramcps.c), equal widths on both sides: a halting local configuration is reached with plain up to width 15, history 1 up to width 20, history 2 up to width 20, history 3 up to width 20, LRU history up to width 6 (larger widths ran out of the 150 s or 60 million configuration budget). n-gram CPS with every cell tagged by its position mod p: fails for p = 2 up to width 16, p = 3 up to width 16, p = 4 up to width 16, p = 6 up to width 16. n-gram CPS where each side also carries the state of a small automaton that has read that side from the far end (every automaton with up to 3 states on both sides, or 4 states on one side), with position mod 1..4 and widths 4, 6, 8: no closed set without a halt in all 120 parameter sets. Run-length windows (the K nearest runs of equal macro cells on each side, run lengths kept exactly below T and mod M above): fails for all 72 parameter sets (cells of 1 to 4 bits, K = 2, 4, 6, T = 2, 4, M = 1, 2, 4). Two-automaton closed tape language by SAT (a deterministic automaton reading each side inward, n states each, CaDiCaL): no solution for n = 2..8; n = 9 not finished in 150 s.
claims.where: sweeps of 13 November 2026 (family F11); the tagged and run-length deciders are not in the repository yet

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Open: the transformation the sweep performs on the string (presumably arithmetic on the number it encodes) is not identified.

claims.title: One sweep pair is the XOR rule
claims.text: Write x = 111 and y = 110. For every word string w over {x, y} ending in y, up to 16 words (65,535 strings): started in B on its first cell the machine sweeps right without turning, rewriting each run 1<sup>m</sup>0 as 0<sup>m−1</sup>11; started in C at the end of that it sweeps left without turning; the result is the word string v with v<sub>i</sub> = w<sub>i</sub> xor w<sub>i+1</sub> (x = 0, y = 1), last word x. This is the linear rule 102 cellular automaton, so every word string can occur and the left string looks random.
claims.where: py/xor_epoch.py, exhaustive per length, run with the machine's own table

claims.title: Defects are walls emitted at the right end
claims.text: Where the word alignment shifts (a run of 1s of length 0 or 1 mod 3, or a double 0) there is a wall between two XOR domains. A single wall survives each epoch and cycles z2 → 13k → 13k−3 → … → 13 → z2, drifting left. A right sweep stops at the first double-0 wall (B reads 0), so walls act like digits of a counter. Walls are created by a 5-phase cycle at the right end, which grows by 2 cells per cycle. A halt needs the token parser (state B) at 1 0 0: a single 1 (seen only within about 30 runs of the right end) followed by 110 words and then a double 0; it was not seen in 3·108 steps.

claims.title: Closed tape language searches (16 November 2026)
claims.text: None closes; each reaches a halting configuration in its abstraction or runs out of budget. Abstract regular model checking over whole-tape automata, merging states by k-step Moore equivalence (forward, reversed, both), k = 1..6, forward from blank and backward from F reading 0. Run-length windows with lengths mod 3 (the F11 sweep tried M = 1, 2, 4 only): K = 2..16 nearest runs with exact lengths below 3 halt; exact lengths up to 4..8, or runs near the blank ends kept exact, exceed 5 to 30 million abstract configurations. The reason found: the bulk is a full shift (any word string), so windows of K runs grow like 2<sup>K</sup>, while the right end needs exact lengths.
claims.where: c/rlwin.cpp (run-length windows); the model-checking scripts are in the project folder ctl-696/tools

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. The left half of the tape is a long string of two 3-cell words, x = 111 and y = 110, and each round trip of the head replaces every word by the XOR of it and its right neighbour: a linear cellular automaton running on the tape. What could make it halt is a defect coming in from the right end.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator.
One round trip on the words 111 = 0, 110 = 1 (every string up to 16 words).

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.505). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.067).
After 109 steps the tape spans 43,577 cells (31,721 left of the start, 197 right), with a density of 1s of 0.805.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: A string of 110s and 111s, run by the XOR rule
html: At step 985,607,083 the head is at the left end and the tape starts A>0 0 1^6 0 1^8 0 1^2 0 1^5 0 1^2 0 1^5 0 1^2 0 1^2 0 1^2 0 1^14 …: runs of 1s whose lengths are 2, 5, 8, 11, 14, … (2 more than a multiple of 3) separated by single 0s. In 3-cell words that is a string over x = 111 and y = 110, about 10,000 words long.

The rule. From the left end the head sweeps right in state B, reading one run at a time: 1^m 0 becomes 0^(m-1) 1 1 (the zigzag B→D→A→B moves one cell right every three steps). At the right it turns and sweeps left in states E, A, B, C, which turns the 0-runs back into 1-runs. Put together, word i of the new string is x if words i and i+1 of the old string were equal and y if they differed:

words
beforey y x y x x x x y y
afterx y y y x x x y x …

With x = 0 and y = 1 that is vi = wi xor wi+1, the linear cellular automaton called rule 102, whose pictures are Sierpinski triangles. py/xor_epoch.py checks it with the machine's own table for every string of up to 16 words. So the string is not a number in some base: it is a linear automaton, and any word string can appear.

Walls. Where the 3-cell alignment shifts (a run of length 0 or 1 mod 3, or a double 0) two XOR domains meet. A single wall survives: it cycles 00 → 1^(3k) → 1^(3k-3) → … → 1^3 → 00 while drifting left. A right sweep stops at the first 00 wall, so the walls behave like the digits of a counter, and the small structure at the right end (a 5-phase cycle that gains 2 cells per cycle) is where new walls come from.

sections.heading: Open
html: The only halt is F reading 0. It needs the right sweep's token reader (state B) to stand on 1 0 0: a run of a single 1, possibly followed by several 110 words read one cell out of step, running into a double-0 wall. Single 1s occur only within about 30 runs of the right end, and this combination was never seen in 3·108 steps.

A closed tape language (a regular set of tapes that contains the start, is closed under a step and has no halt) would settle it, and was searched for on 16 November 2026 with whole-tape automata and with run-length windows that count lengths mod 3; none closed. The bulk can hold any word string, so local windows explode, while the walls near the right end need exact lengths. A language that keeps the right end exact and lets the bulk be any word string with walls is the next thing to try.

summary: The left side is a long string of the 3-cell words 111 and 110; each round trip of the head replaces every word by the XOR of it and its right neighbour (rule 102), and defects (walls) come in from a small cycling structure at the right end. No closed tape language found yet.
